notes.b: Choose equipment for the quantity of food, the cooking method and the type of hob, and check how the material conducts heat.
points: A heavy, thick base spreads heat evenly and reduces hot spots that scorch food; a thin base heats unevenly.
Aluminium and copper conduct heat quickly; stainless steel is durable and does not react with acidic foods, but it conducts heat less well unless the base is bonded to copper or aluminium.
Cast iron retains heat well and suits slow, even cooking such as braising, but it is heavy and rusts if left damp.
A non-stick coating allows frying with little fat, but it is damaged by overheating an empty pan and by metal utensils.
A close-fitting lid retains steam, so food simmers with less energy and in less time.
A pan base should match the ring size, so that the full base makes contact with the heat source.
Induction hobs need pans with a magnetic base; aluminium and copper pans without one will not heat.
Handles should be heat-resistant and firmly fixed; plastic and wooden handles are not suitable for the oven unless the manufacturer states it.
A cook's knife is used for general chopping, a serrated knife for bread and soft-skinned foods, and a paring knife for small, detailed work.
A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one because it cuts with less force and is less likely to slip.
The claw grip curls the fingertips of the guiding hand under, so the knuckles guide the blade and the fingertips stay clear of it.
Place the chopping board on a damp cloth or non-slip mat so that it cannot move while cutting.
Colour-coded boards keep raw meat, raw vegetables and ready-to-eat foods apart, preventing cross-contamination.
Carry a knife by its handle with the blade pointing down and away from the body; never leave a knife in a sink of water.
Store knives in a block, on a rack or on a magnetic strip, so that the edges are protected and the blades are not loose in a drawer.

notes.h: Safe use of the hob, oven and electrical appliances
points: Turn pan handles inwards over the hob so they cannot be knocked or pulled, and never leave hot oil unattended.
Lift lids away from the face so that escaping steam does not scald.
Use oven gloves or a dry cloth to handle hot dishes; a damp cloth conducts heat and causes scalds.
Keep the flex of electrical appliances away from hot surfaces and water, and never handle an appliance with wet hands.
Switch off and unplug an appliance before cleaning its blades or removing food from them.
Do not use an appliance with a damaged flex or plug; it must be repaired or replaced before use.
Pressure cooker: check that the sealing ring and valve are clean and undamaged, and never open the lid until the pressure has been released.
Microwave: use containers marked as microwave-safe and never place metal in the cavity.
Wash equipment in hot soapy water or in a dishwasher, then rinse and dry it thoroughly before storing it, so that bacteria cannot grow in damp areas.
Do not run cold water into a hot pan; the sudden change in temperature can warp the base and crack a non-stick or ceramic surface.
Cast iron must be dried straight after washing and wiped with a thin film of oil to prevent rust.
Wooden or silicone utensils protect non-stick surfaces, whereas metal utensils scratch them.
Use abrasive pads only on surfaces that tolerate them; stainless steel and cast iron tolerate them better than non-stick coatings.
Dishcloths, sponges and tea towels can carry bacteria and should be changed or washed regularly.

keyTerms.definition: The transfer of bacteria from raw food, hands or equipment to food that is ready to eat.
A knife-handling technique in which the fingertips of the guiding hand are curled under so that the knuckles guide the blade.
A pan with a thick base that spreads heat evenly across the cooking surface and reduces hot spots.
A surface on a pan that prevents food sticking, allowing cooking with little fat, but damaged by overheating and metal utensils.
A heavy metal used for cookware that retains heat well and must be dried and oiled to prevent rust.
A knife with a toothed edge used for cutting bread and soft-skinned foods.
A sealed pan that cooks food quickly under steam pressure and must not be opened until the pressure is released.
Describes a container marked as suitable for microwave use and containing no metal.
A hob that heats magnetic pans directly through electromagnetic induction, so only pans with a magnetic base can be used.

factCards.term: Three knife types for kitchen use
factCards.definition: Cook's knife for general chopping; serrated knife for bread and soft-skinned foods; paring knife for small, detailed work.

factCards.term: Three rules for carrying a knife
factCards.definition: Point the blade down and away from the body; carry it by the handle at the side; never try to catch a falling knife.

factCards.term: Four ways to prevent cross-contamination in the kitchen
factCards.definition: Use separate colour-coded chopping boards for raw and cooked foods; wash hands after handling raw meat; store raw meat below ready-to-eat food in the fridge; clean and sanitise equipment between tasks.

factCards.term: Three care rules for cast iron
factCards.definition: Dry it straight after washing; wipe it with a thin film of oil; never leave it soaking or damp.

factCards.term: Two things that damage a non-stick coating
factCards.definition: Overheating an empty pan, and scraping the surface with metal utensils.

factCards.term: Two checks before using a pressure cooker
factCards.definition: That the sealing ring and the valve are clean and undamaged; that the lid is locked on correctly before heating.

questions.prompt: Outline three factors to consider when selecting a saucepan for use on an induction hob.
questions.model: Base material: the pan must have a magnetic base, otherwise it will not heat on an induction hob. Base thickness: a heavy, thick base spreads heat evenly and reduces hot spots. Size: the pan base should match the ring size so that the full base makes contact with the hob. A close-fitting lid retains steam and reduces cooking time and energy. Heat-resistant handles that are firmly fixed make the pan safe to lift and move.

questions.prompt: Explain how a non-stick frying pan and a wooden chopping board should be used and cared for so that they stay safe and hygienic.
questions.model: Non-stick pan: avoid overheating an empty pan, as this damages the coating. Use wooden or silicone utensils, because metal scratches the surface. Allow the pan to cool before washing it, since cold water on a hot pan can warp the base or crack the coating. Wash in hot soapy water, rinse and dry before storing. Chopping board: place it on a damp cloth or non-slip mat so it does not move while cutting. Keep it separate from raw meat and ready-to-eat foods, using a colour-coded board for each. Wash in hot soapy water after each use, dry thoroughly and store upright so air can circulate. Replace boards that become deeply cut or grooved, because bacteria can collect in the cuts.
